subtitle: Thursday, 5 November 2026
editor_note: This edition looks at how AI is reshaping the physical, commercial, and educational foundations of our digital world. From the data centres that power AI and the growing role of open-source models, to the tensions emerging between technology providers and schools, these stories highlight questions of responsibility, choice, and control that matter for anyone planning for workforce and public-service needs. We hope these summaries help you connect global developments to Tamkeen's mission.

items.title: Setting a new standard for responsible AI infrastructure
items.summary: OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, has published two new frameworks aimed at guiding how large AI data centres — the massive facilities that provide the computing power for AI — are built in local communities. The 'National Community Compact' and 'Compute Campus Policy Blueprint' set out commitments to protect local resources such as water and electricity, create local jobs, and work transparently with host communities. The move responds to growing public concern about the environmental and economic impact of the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure. For government bodies, these documents offer a practical reference point for negotiating with technology firms and setting conditions that protect public interests. As Gulf nations invest heavily in AI computing capacity, such standards are relevant to how similar projects could be managed responsibly in the region.

items.title: Open source AI is booming. Hugging Face explains who profits.
items.summary: This TechCrunch discussion, featuring leaders from Hugging Face (a major platform for sharing AI models), examines the rapid rise of 'open source' AI — models that are made freely available for anyone to use, adapt, and run themselves. Enterprises, governments, and startups are increasingly drawn to these open models because they can lower costs, offer greater control over data, and allow more customisation than closed commercial systems. The conversation raises a key business question: if powerful models are free, how do companies actually make money from them? It also notes that Chinese open models are becoming highly competitive, raising questions about which countries and firms will lead this field. For public-sector organisations, open models are notable because they can reduce dependence on any single foreign vendor and allow more sovereign control over technology.

items.title: DuckDuckGo pitches itself to schools amid backlash over Google’s AI policy
items.summary: Search engine DuckDuckGo is actively marketing itself to schools that are unhappy with Google's approach to AI features in its services. The company is highlighting its privacy-focused search tools and the ability to turn off AI functions entirely — an option some educators want in order to maintain control over what students access. This reflects a wider debate in education about how much AI should be embedded in the everyday tools used in classrooms, and who gets to decide. The story shows that schools are becoming an important battleground for technology providers competing on different values, such as privacy and user choice. For those working in education and human-capital development, it is a reminder that the choice of digital tools carries real policy and governance implications.

items.title: Building on open source AI? Hugging Face’s policy chief on the costs, risks, and trade-offs
items.summary: In this companion podcast episode, Hugging Face's policy chief explores the practical realities of building products and services on top of open-source AI models. While open models offer cost savings, flexibility, and greater control, the discussion stresses that they also come with trade-offs — including the responsibility to manage safety, security, and ongoing maintenance that a vendor might otherwise handle. The conversation also touches on competition between American and Chinese open models and what that means for the global AI landscape. This perspective is valuable for governments and institutions considering open models, as it clarifies that 'free' does not mean 'without cost or risk.' Understanding these trade-offs is important for any organisation weighing how to adopt AI responsibly and sustainably.

items.title: Google faces backlash for plan that would turn off Search for schools that restrict AI
items.summary: Google is facing significant criticism over a reported plan that would switch off its Search service for schools that choose to restrict certain AI features. Prominent public figures, including New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani and former US regulator Lina Khan, have accused the company of behaving like an unregulated monopoly by using its dominance in search to pressure schools into accepting its AI tools. The backlash highlights concerns about how much power large technology companies hold over essential digital services that institutions depend on daily. For public-sector bodies, this episode underscores the risks of becoming overly reliant on a single provider, and the importance of having clear policies and alternatives. It also illustrates why AI governance and competition rules are drawing increasing attention from policymakers worldwide.
